summary: Heather Stoddard is a scholar of Tibetology and history/archaeology. She studied at SOAS University of London (~1967–1970) and under Nicole Vandier-Nicolas, D. C. Lau, and Samten Gyaltsen Karmay.

Heeraman Tiwari is an Indologist and philosopher. He studied at the universities of Lucknow, Delhi, and Oxford under Bimal Krishna Matilal and Richard Gombrich, later holding posts at Jawaharlal Nehru University, Heidelberg University, and Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Hegoda Khemananda is a Buddhist studies scholar who served as Vice Principal of Vidyodaya Pirivena and Director of Dharma Paryeshanalaya, both attested in 1993.

Heidi Fjeld is a scholar of Tibetology and religious studies. She earned her Doctor Rerum Politicarum under Signe Howell at the University of Oslo (~2001–2006), where she later served as a postdoctoral fellow (~2007–2010).
Heidi I. Köppl is a scholar in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. She earned an MA at the University of Copenhagen under Christian K. Wedemeyer and also studied under Khenpo Sherab Zangpo.

Heidi Pauwels is a scholar of Indology and religious studies. She studied at KU Leuven, Vrindaban Research Institute, Cologne, and the University of Washington under Alan W. Entwistle, later holding posts at SOAS and the University of Washington.

Heike Oberlin is an Indologist who studied at the University of Tübingen, Kerala Kalamandalam, and the University of Würzburg. She held academic posts at Tübingen (2005–2008), Kerala Kalamandalam (2018), and the University of Rome (2025).

Heiner Eichner was a scholar of linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied under Karl Hoffmann at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (~1964–1974) and held a post at the University of Vienna (~1989–2010).
Heinrich August Jäschke was a linguist and Tibetologist. He served as co-director at Pädagogium Niesky (1847) and as a missionary for the Moravian Church and its Kyelang mission (~1857–1868).

Heinrich Blochmann was a scholar of Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and history. Educated at Leipzig, Paris, and Calcutta, he held posts at Doveton College, Fort William College, The Asiatic Society, and Aliah University.
Heinrich Brunn was a scholar of history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Bonn (~1839–1843) and later held a post at the University of Munich (~1865–1894).

Heinrich Ewald was a scholar of linguistics, Indology, and religious studies. He studied at the Große Schule and the University of Göttingen, where he later served as professor alongside a professorship at the University of Tübingen.

Heinrich Hettrich was a scholar of linguistics and Indology who studied at Saarland University and the University of Giessen. He held academic posts at Munich, Marburg, Salzburg, Zurich, and Würzburg, where he held the chair in comparative linguistics.

Heinrich Hübschmann was a linguist, Indologist, and Iranian and Central Asian studies scholar. He studied at Jena, Tübingen, Munich (under Martin Haug), and Leipzig, and held professorships at the universities of Leipzig and Strasbourg.

Heinrich Kiepert was a geographer and historian who studied at the University of Berlin and the University of Jena. He held posts at the Landes-Industrie-Comptoir in Weimar and served as professor of geography at the University of Berlin.

Heinrich Leberecht Fleischer was an Orientalist and linguist. He studied at the University of Leipzig and under Silvestre de Sacy and Chézy in Paris, later holding the chair of Oriental languages at Leipzig from 1836.

Heinrich Lüders was an Indologist and linguist. Educated at Munich and Göttingen under Franz Kielhorn, he held posts at Oxford, Göttingen, Rostock, Kiel, the Prussian Academy of Sciences, and the University of Berlin.

Heinrich Rickert was a philosopher who studied at the universities of Berlin and Strasbourg. He held academic posts at the University of Freiburg (~1891–1916) and the University of Heidelberg (~1916–1932).
Heinrich Rückert was a scholar of history, archaeology, and linguistics. He held academic posts at the University of Jena (~1845–1852) and the University of Breslau (~1852–1875).
Heinrich Schliemann was an archaeologist and historian. He pursued studies at the University of Paris from 1866 to 1868 and at the University of Rostock in ~1869.
